title: How to scope an MVP: guide for Indian startups

contentHtml:
What an MVP actually is

In short: An MVP is the smallest version of your product that lets you learn whether real customers want it, not the smallest app you can afford. Scope it by writing down the one job it must do, sorting every feature with MoSCoW, keeping Must Haves to about 60% of the effort, and getting a written scope priced before anyone writes code.

The term comes from Eric Ries. In a post on his blog dated 3 August 2009, he defined the minimum viable product as "that version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort." In the same post he wrote that "MVP, despite the name, is not about creating minimal products."

That second line is the one founders skip. The Lean Startup principles describe a startup's basic activity as turning ideas into products, measuring how customers respond, and learning whether to pivot or persevere. The MVP is the first turn of that loop. If it cannot tell you something you did not know, it is too small, however little it cost.

If you want your scope and cost written down before you commit, this is what our ₹3,500 requirement analysis produces: a call with the people who would build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline before any build starts (how it works). The rest of this post needs nothing from us.

This guide was checked in November 2026, against Startup India's recognition pages and the Agile Business Consortium's MoSCoW guidance. Government scheme details change, so check the linked pages before you apply for anything.

Must-have vs later: the four MoSCoW buckets

MoSCoW is a way of sorting requirements that comes from DSDM, the agile framework whose guidance the Agile Business Consortium publishes. Its four buckets are below, in the consortium's own words where it gives them.

The four MoSCoW buckets and what they mean for an MVP

BucketAgile Business Consortium definitionWhat it means for your MVP
Must HaveThe Minimum Usable SubseT (MUST) of requirements which the project guarantees to deliverWithout it, the product cannot do its one job or cannot legally go live
Should HaveImportant but not vitalPainful to leave out, but there is a workaround for now
Could HaveWanted or desirable but less importantThe first thing to drop when time runs short
Won't Have this timeRequirements the project team has agreed will not be delivered in this timeframeWritten down on purpose, so nobody asks again mid-build

Source: Agile Business Consortium, What is MoSCoW prioritization, read 16 November 2026.

The guidance that makes MoSCoW work is about effort, not about counting features. The consortium says Must Have effort should not exceed 60% of the total, with a pool of Could Haves typically around 20%. The point of that split is a buffer: if estimates turn out wrong, the team drops Could Haves and still ships every Must.

An MVP where every feature is a Must Have has no buffer at all. Any delay becomes a missed date, and any missed date becomes an argument.

A quick test for every feature

When a founder sends me a feature list, I ask four questions of each line. They are mine, not part of any framework, but they map onto the buckets.

  • Does the core job fail without it? A booking app without booking fails. A booking app without a referral programme does not. Yes means Must Have.
  • Will a real user hit it in their first week? If not, it can wait for the second release.
  • Is there a manual workaround? Admins approving accounts by hand, invoices sent from your accounting software, reports pulled into a spreadsheet. If a person can do it for the first hundred customers, it is a Should or Could.
  • Does it help you learn the thing you are testing? If the MVP exists to test whether clinics will pay, payment collection is a Must. A dashboard of vanity numbers is not.

The manual workaround question removes more scope than the other three together. Many 'must have' admin panels are really a founder not wanting to do something by hand for three months.

Writing a scope document a developer can price

A feature list is not a scope. Two developers can read 'user login' and quote very different amounts, because one pictures phone OTP and the other pictures OTP, Google sign-in, password reset and account deletion. A scope document closes that gap.

What I would put in one, in this order:

  1. The one job. One sentence: who uses it, to do what, instead of what they do today.
  2. Users and roles. Customer, staff, admin. What each can see and change.
  3. Screens or flows. Each Must Have as a short flow: what the user taps, what they see, what happens next. Rough sketches on paper are fine.
  4. Integrations. Payment gateway, SMS or WhatsApp, maps, an existing ERP or accounting tool. Each one named, because each one is work.
  5. Platforms. Android, iPhone, web, or which of them first.
  6. Won't Have list. The features you have agreed to leave out. This list is what protects the price.
  7. Acceptance. How you will decide each feature is done, in plain words a non-developer can test.
  8. Ownership. Code, cloud accounts and app store accounts in your company's name from day one.

How a developer turns this into hours is its own subject; our post on estimating software honestly explains what a good estimate shows its working on.

Step by step: scoping your MVP in a week

This is the order I would do it in, one step a day or so, before talking to anyone about price.

Step 1. Write the one job and the one question. The job is what the product does. The question is what you need to learn from it, such as 'will 20 clinics pay a monthly fee to take bookings online?'

Step 2. List every feature anyone has mentioned. Yours, your co-founder's, an investor's, a competitor's. Do not argue yet.

Step 3. Run the four-question test on each line. Mark each as Must, Should, Could or Won't.

Step 4. Cut Musts until they feel uncomfortable. If more than about half the list is Must Have, you have not finished. Push features to Should where a manual workaround exists.

Step 5. Sketch the Must Have flows. On paper or in a design tool. Every screen you cannot draw is a decision you have not made.

Step 6. Write the scope document. Use the eight sections above. Put the Won't Have list in the same document, not in your head.

Step 7. Get it priced as written, by more than one team. Ask each to list what they assumed. Differences in assumptions tell you more than differences in price.

Fixed price or time and materials

Once the scope is written, you choose how to pay for it. There are two common models, and neither is always right.

Fixed price and time and materials, compared for an MVP

Fixed priceTime and materials
What you agreeA scope, a price and a timelineA rate per hour or month, and a team
Who carries estimate riskMostly the developer, within the agreed scopeMostly you
How change is handledA written change request, priced separatelyAbsorbed into the next weeks of work, and the bill
Works best whenScope is written down and stableScope is genuinely unknown, such as research or a prototype
Main risk for youQuality cut to protect the price, or arguments over what was 'in scope'No natural end date, cost that grows with indecision
What protects youA detailed scope and a Won't Have listWeekly demos, a budget cap and the right to stop

For a first MVP built by an outside team, I lean towards fixed price on a written scope, because it forces the scoping work to happen before money is spent. Time and materials suits a team you already trust, or work where nobody can write the scope yet. In that case, cap it: a fixed number of weeks, then a decision.

Whichever you choose, the contract should say who owns the code, the cloud accounts and the app store listings. With us, those stay in the client's name; ask any team you talk to the same question.

What an MVP costs, and what moves the number

I am not going to give a single rupee figure for an MVP, because I would be making it up. The price is the hours your scope needs multiplied by the team's rate, and both vary widely. What I can tell you is what moves the hours:

  • Number of user roles. A customer app plus a staff app plus an admin panel is three products sharing a database.
  • Platforms. Android and iPhone from one cross-platform codebase often costs less than two native apps; our Flutter vs React Native post covers the trade-off.
  • Integrations. Each payment gateway, messaging provider or existing system adds testing and failure cases.
  • Real-time features. Live tracking, chat and live dashboards cost more than screens that refresh when you open them.
  • Unclear scope. The most expensive item of all, because it shows up as rework.

For the ranges we have seen and how they break down by app type, read our mobile app development cost guide for India. Then budget for running costs after launch, which are not part of the build price.

Startup India recognition: what helps an early founder

DPIIT recognition under Startup India is free and worth checking before you spend on the build, because some of its benefits bite in the first years. The recognition page on startupindia.gov.in sets these eligibility rules:

  • Incorporated as a private limited company, or registered as a partnership firm, LLP or cooperative society.
  • Turnover below ₹200 crore (₹300 crore for DeepTech startups) in every previous financial year.
  • Counted as a startup for up to 10 years from incorporation (20 years for DeepTech).
  • Working towards innovation or improvement of products, services or processes, with potential to create jobs or wealth. A business formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing one does not qualify.

You apply through the National Single Window System by adding the form "Registration as a Startup". The same page says the Ministry of Commerce and Industry charges no fee for recognition and has not appointed any agency or representative for it, so anyone selling you "DPIIT registration" is selling form-filling.

The benefits most relevant to an early founder, from the Startup India scheme page and the recognition page:

  • Income tax holiday under Section 80-IAC. After recognition, a startup can apply for a tax holiday for 3 consecutive financial years out of its first ten. Only private limited companies and LLPs incorporated after 1 April 2016 are eligible, and it is a separate application.
  • Self-certification. The scheme page says startups can self-certify compliance with 6 labour laws and 3 environmental laws online, with no labour law inspections for 5 years. I saw other official documents give a different count of labour laws, so check the current list for your case.
  • Patent fees. The scheme page says startups get an 80% rebate on patent filing fees compared with other companies, plus fast-tracked patent applications.
  • Winding up. Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, startups with simple debt structures can be wound up within 90 days of applying.
  • Public procurement. The scheme page says manufacturing startups are exempt from 'prior experience or turnover' criteria in government tenders, without relaxing quality standards.

The recognition page also links to an exemption under Section 56 of the Income Tax Act, often called angel tax. Tax rules on this have changed in recent budgets, so ask your CA whether it still matters for your fundraise before you count on it.

None of this changes how you scope the MVP. It changes when you incorporate and in what form, which is worth deciding before you sign a build contract in a company's name.

Three worked examples

These products and feature lists are made up to show the method. They are not real clients or real figures.

A clinic booking app

Illustrative. The one job: patients book a slot with a doctor at a two-doctor clinic without calling. The question: will patients book online if the clinic shares a link on WhatsApp?

Must Have: doctor availability, slot booking, booking confirmation, a staff view of the day's bookings. Should Have: reminders the day before, cancellation by the patient. Could Have: online payment at booking. Won't Have this time: video consultations, patient records, multiple branches. Payment drops to Could because the test is about booking, and patients can pay at the counter for now.

A distributor's ordering app

Illustrative. The one job: shopkeepers reorder stock from a distributor on their phone instead of calling a salesman. The question: will shopkeepers place repeat orders without a call?

Must Have: product list with the shop's own prices, cart, order placement, an order list for the distributor's staff. Should Have: order status updates. Could Have: credit limit display. Won't Have this time: online payment, delivery tracking, sync with the distributor's accounting software. The accounting sync is the trap here: it feels essential, but staff can enter orders by hand for the first months while you find out if shopkeepers use the app at all.

A coaching institute app

Illustrative. The one job: students of one institute see their batch timetable, notes and test scores in one place. The question: do students open it weekly without being told to?

Must Have: phone login, batch timetable, notes as PDFs, test scores entered by staff. Should Have: announcements. Could Have: doubt-posting. Won't Have this time: live classes, fee payment, a parent app. Live classes are the feature most likely to sneak back in, and they would roughly turn this into a different product.

Six scope-creep traps

The investor feature. Someone on a call suggests AI, a marketplace or a referral system. It goes on the list as a Should or Won't, with a note of who asked, not into the build.

The admin panel that grows. Reports, exports, filters and role permissions for a team of two. Start with the smallest admin that lets staff do the Must Have flows.

'While you are in there.' Small requests made during the build, each reasonable, together a month of work. Collect them in one list and price them together after launch.

Building for scale you do not have. Designing for a million users before you have a hundred. Sensible foundations, yes; our tech stack post covers that, but load testing for a launch to fifty clinics is not an MVP job.

Copying a competitor's feature list. Their product is years old. Their feature list is the result of what they learnt, not where they started.

No Won't Have list. If the scope only says what is in, everything not mentioned becomes an argument. Writing down what is out is the cheapest protection you have.

A one-page scope checklist

Before you send your scope to anyone for a price, check it against this.

MVP scope checklist

CheckDone when
One job, one questionBoth fit in one sentence each
MoSCoW sortEvery feature has a bucket, and Musts are roughly 60% of the effort or less
Manual workaroundsEvery Should and Could has a note on how you will manage without it
Flows sketchedEvery Must Have has a screen-by-screen flow
Integrations namedEach third-party service is listed with what it does
Won't Have listWritten in the same document, agreed by all founders
Acceptance testsEach Must Have has a plain-words test you can run yourself
OwnershipCode, cloud and store accounts in the company's name
Company formIncorporation and DPIIT eligibility checked before signing

If you would like a team to do this with you rather than for you, our MVP development page describes how we work.

Frequently asked questions

What is an MVP in simple words?

It is the first version of a product that lets you learn whether customers want it, with the least effort. Eric Ries, who popularised the term, defined it in 2009 as the version that collects the maximum validated learning about customers with the least effort, and wrote that it is not about creating minimal products.

How many features should an MVP have?

There is no right number. What matters is effort: the Agile Business Consortium's MoSCoW guidance says Must Have effort should not exceed 60% of the total, with around 20% in Could Haves you can drop if estimates slip.

What does MoSCoW stand for?

Must Have, Should Have, Could Have and Won't Have this time. The Agile Business Consortium says MUST stands for Minimum Usable SubseT.

Should I choose fixed price or time and materials for my MVP?

For a first MVP built by an outside team, I lean towards fixed price on a written scope, because it forces the scoping to happen first. Time and materials suits work nobody can scope yet; cap it by weeks and budget.

How much does an MVP cost in India?

It depends on hours and rate, and the hours depend on user roles, platforms, integrations and how clear the scope is. I do not quote a single figure without a scope. Write the scope first and get it priced by more than one team.

Do I need DPIIT recognition before building an MVP?

No, but check eligibility early. Recognition is free, applied for through the National Single Window System, and some benefits, such as the 80-IAC tax holiday, need a private limited company or LLP incorporated after 1 April 2016.

Who should own the code of my MVP?

Your company. The contract should say that code, cloud accounts and app store accounts are in your company's name from the start, whoever builds it.
